answers: Chart of accounts, counterparties (us, customers, suppliers), catalogue items, warehouse locations, VAT rates — each gets its own master-data object.

So when we're talking about our master data, what we've got is the chart of accounts living in one master-data object, then the companies we deal with — that's ourselves, our customers, and our suppliers — all sitting in their own master-data object, and then on top of that we've got the catalogue items in another one, the warehouse locations in another one, and finally the VAT rates each getting their own master-data object too.
Each of these gets its own master-data object: the chart of accounts, the companies we deal with (ourselves, customers, suppliers), the catalogue items, the warehouse locations, and the VAT rates.

Sales invoices we issue are recorded as sales_invoice documents with these fields pulled from the invoice: number, issue date, seller and buyer (looked up by NIP), net amount, currency, and VAT rate code. VAT = net × rate% ÷ 100, rounded half up to the grosz; gross = net + VAT; due date = issue date + payment days from the invoice; status begins as open and may change to paid. Booking goes into pl-stat: debit 201 for gross, credit 700 for net, credit 222 for VAT.

So whenever we send out a sales invoice, it gets created in the system as a document of type sales_invoice, and we fill in the number, the issue date, the seller and the buyer — both identified by their NIP — plus the net amount, the currency, and the VAT rate code, all straight off the invoice itself. Then the VAT is worked out by multiplying the net by the rate's percentage and dividing by 100, and we round that half up to the nearest grosz, the gross is just net plus that VAT, and the due date is whatever the issue date is with the payment days printed on the invoice added on top. The status kicks off as open and can later flip to paid. When we post it to the books, it all goes into pl-stat: account 201 gets debited with the gross, account 700 gets credited with the net, and account 222 gets credited with the VAT.

Every invoice we put out? That's a sales_invoice document — grabs the number, issue date, seller, buyer (both by NIP), net amount, currency, and VAT rate code right off the paper. VAT gets calculated as net times the rate percent over 100, rounded half up to the grosz; add that to the net and you've got the gross; slap the payment days from the invoice onto the issue date and that's your due date; status is open to start, goes to paid later. Posts to pl-stat: 201 debited with gross, 700 credited with net, 222 credited with VAT.

Each delivery produces exactly one PZ document — type pz — carrying the supplier, the supplier's delivery document number, the warehouse location, the date, and the currency. Each item on that delivery becomes a pz_line tied to the PZ, holding qty, price, and value, where value equals qty times the unit price from the delivery. Every pz_line moves the item's stock into the location on the PZ and posts to book pl-stat: debit 330, credit 300, at that line's value.

So whenever a delivery comes in, you create one PZ document — that's a new type called pz — and on it you record the supplier, the supplier's delivery document number, the warehouse location, the date, and the currency, all of that on every single PZ. Then for each item that arrived, you add a line to that PZ — a new type called pz_line — and each of those lines points back to its PZ and has three fields on it: qty, price, and value, and that value is just the quantity multiplied by the unit price as stated on the delivery, nothing fancy. Each one of those lines does two things: it pushes the item's stock into whichever warehouse location is on the PZ, and it fires off a posting in the book pl-stat, debit account 330, credit account 300, for the value of that line.

One delivery, one PZ — type pz — with the supplier, supplier's delivery doc number, warehouse location, date, and currency on it. Every item in that delivery gets its own pz_line hanging off that PZ, with qty, price, and value fields; value is qty times the unit price from the delivery. That pz_line stocks the item into the PZ's location and books it in pl-stat, debit 330, credit 300, at the line's value.

A supplier invoice maps to a purchase_invoice document with these fields: number, invoice date, supplier looked up by NIP, our company as owner, net amount, currency, and VAT rate code. VAT = net × rate% ÷ 100, rounded half up to the grosz; gross = net + VAT. Book it in pl-stat: debit 300 for net, debit 221 for VAT, credit 202 for gross.

So what happens is, when a supplier sends us an invoice, we create a document of type purchase_invoice, and on that document we record the number, the invoice date, we look up the supplier using their NIP, we set our own company as the owner, and then we've got the net amount, the currency, and the VAT rate code. Now the VAT itself is calculated by taking the net, multiplying it by whatever percent belongs to that rate code, dividing by 100, and rounding half up to the grosz, and then the gross is just net plus that VAT. Every single one of these purchase invoices then gets posted into the pl-stat book, where we debit account 300 with the net, debit account 221 with the VAT, and credit account 202 with the gross.

Each supplier invoice turns into a purchase_invoice — grab the number, invoice date, match the supplier by NIP, put our company down as owner, then net amount, currency, VAT rate code. A goods_issue document (fields: item, location, quantity, date, reason) is created each time goods leave the warehouse, and each one reduces that item's stock at its location.

So when stuff goes out of the warehouse, right, the system makes a goods_issue — it's got the item, location, quantity, date, and reason on it — and that knocks the stock for that item out of its location.
Each warehouse outflow generates a document of type goods_issue carrying the item, location, quantity, date, and reason, and the act of issuing removes that item's stock from its location.
A sales invoice gets marked paid when a bank statement line's reference matches its number.

So basically what happens is, if you've got a bank statement line and its reference field contains one of our sales invoice numbers, then that invoice is going to get flipped over to paid status automatically.
When the reference on a bank statement line matches one of our sales invoice numbers, that invoice gets marked as paid.

Complaints get logged as complaint docs holding a number, customer, and details. Each one automatically kicks off a case — type named case, subject set to the complaint number, status beginning at open and movable to resolved.

So what happens is this: when a complaint comes in, you create a complaint document that captures the number, the customer, and the details. That complaint document then triggers the creation of a follow-up case, and this case has a type called case, its subject is populated with the complaint number, its status starts out as open, and down the line that status can be changed to resolved.

Each complaint lands as a complaint document — number, customer, details — and spins up a linked case straight away, type name case, subject being the complaint number, status kicking off at open and shifting to resolved later.
A withdrawn complaint gets its case closed as resolved.
So basically, if the customer decides to pull back their complaint, what happens is that the case tied to it ends up being marked as resolved.
Customer pulls the complaint — case goes to resolved.

A stock count for an item at a location creates a stock_level record with four fields: date, counted, book, and difference. Date is the count date, counted is the counted quantity, book is the sum of that item's inbound stock movements at the location minus outbound ones up to and including the count date, and difference is counted minus book.

So when you do a stock count for an item at a location, what you're actually storing is a new type called stock_level, and it's got these four fields on it — date, counted, book, and difference — where date is the count date, counted is just the counted quantity, book is calculated as all the stock movements bringing that item into the location added up and then the ones taking it out subtracted, but only movements dated up to and including the count date, and then difference is simply counted minus book.

For a stock count of an item at a location, you log a stock_level — that's the type name — carrying date, counted, book, and difference: the count date, the counted quantity, the book quantity being inbound stock movements for that item at that location minus outbound ones dated through and including the count date, and difference being counted minus book.
